title: Enhanced performance of magnetoelectric energy harvester based on compound magnetic coupling effect

sections.heading: Enhanced performance of magnetoelectric energy harvester based on compound magnetic coupling effect
sections.text:
Jinchi Han,1 Jun Hu,2,a) Zhongxu Wang,1 Shan X. Wang,1,2 and Jinliang He1,a) 1 The State Key Lab of Power System, Department of Electrical Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China 2 Center for Magnetic Nanotechnology, Stanford University, 450 Serra Mall, Stanford, California 94305, USA (Received 23 December 2014; accepted 28 March 2015; published online 8 April 2015)

We have theoretically and experimentally demonstrated the greatly enhanced energy harvesting property of the specific magnetoelectric (ME) device, comprising a piezoelectric bimorph cantilever with a permanent magnet tip mass based on a compound interaction between the remanent magnetic moment of the magnet and a nonuniform alternating magnetic field. With appropriate positioning of the device, the coexistence of torque-mode and force-mode excitations leads to reinforced magnetomechanical coupling, which subsequently yields improvements in both ME response and power conversion. In the experiments, a piezoelectric bimorph/magnet energy harvester was placed at a distance of $1 0 \mathrm { m m }$ from a power line that was conducting a $5 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , $1 0 \mathrm { A }$ current, and a maximum power of $2 . 1 3 6 \mathrm { m W }$ was achieved via the optimal cooperative magnetic coupling mode. This output power is $7 . 8 \times$ larger than that produced using the conventional torque mode. $©$ 2015 AIP Publishing LLC. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1063/1.4917214]

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The vision of a smart world with easy access to various information sources and abundant data to assist with decision-making is both exciting and inspiring. Consequently, ubiquitous sensing based on miniaturized, reliable, and maintenance-free sensor nodes is increasingly attractive because it offers the prospect of comprehensive monitoring and data-collection in both industrial and residential scenarios, and thus caters for and promotes the upsurge of development of the Internet of Things, intelligent building management systems, and wide-area measurement systems in the smart grid. Energy constraint, however, typically forms one of the most important challenges for these massive applications at present.1 Recent developments in energy harvesting technology have paved the way for the emergence of self-sustaining sensors that are capable of scavenging energy from the environment. In addition to the ambient vibrational energy that has drawn a great deal of scientific research interest,2–6 lowfrequency alternating magnetic fields also represent a promising energy source, because current-carrying power lines are extensively distributed and are accessible almost everywhere. For certain specific applications, such as on-line metering systems for the smart grid or appliance load monitoring in building management systems, the power-frequency magnetic field represents a more favorable energy source option than stochastic vibration sources because of the stability and intensity of the power supply.

The conventional method to convert magnetic energy into electrical energy is based on electromagnetic induction. Despite satisfactory efficiency in high-frequency applications,7 a moderately sized coreless pick-up coil is ineffective for harvesting of low-frequency magnetic fields. The flourish of multiferroic magnetoelectric (ME) composites, which consist of a magnetostrictive phase and a piezoelectric phase, has provided an innovative route to realize the same type of energy conversion,8,9 and the capabilities of these materials for harvesting of high-frequency magnetic energy have been used for various objectives.10–12 However, these materials generally have high resonance frequencies (usually the kilohertz range), and the mismatch between these resonance frequencies and the low frequency characteristics of ambient stray alternating magnetic field usually leads to extremely low voltage and power output performances.

ME devices based on a piezoelectric bimorph cantilever and a permanent magnet tip mass, which were first proposed by Xing et al.,13 have demonstrated remarkable ME responses14,15 and outstanding energy harvesting properties16 at low frequencies. These devices used torque-mode magnetic coupling for excitation, which originated from the forced alignment of the remanent moment with the external AC magnetic field. In addition to the torque-mode coupling, previous works have also involved the magnetic force experienced by the tip magnets in the non-uniform fields.17–19 Among these works, He et al. used a Halbach array to enhance the reactive ampere force acting on the magnet, and achieved $5 6 6 \mu \mathrm { W }$ output from a single wire conducting a current of 10 A.18 Comparisons were made between the energy harvesting properties of devices based on torque-mode and force-mode magnetic coupling, and a piezoelectric/magnet device based on torque-mode coupling performed more efficiently when harvesting stray magnetic energy than a device based on force-mode coupling.19 However, the conventional magnetic torque coupling mode is far from the best option in the context of practical applications, e.g., scavenging energy from $5 0 \mathrm { H z }$ or $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ power lines. When the non-uniform AC magnetic field distributed around the power line is considered, torque-mode and force-mode excitations actually coexist for the ME cantilever. In this paper, the compound interaction between the magnetic force coupling and the magnetic torque coupling is analyzed using our established magneto-mechanical coupling model. An optimal cooperative magnetic coupling effect is predicted theoretically and is experimentally verified by the dramatically enhanced performance of the fabricated ME energy harvester. The proposed method may also inspire other types of ME devices to use the cooperative effect of these two conventional coupling modes under a non-uniform magnetic field, which has shown outstanding merit in pursuit of superior performance.

sections.heading: II. THEORETICAL ANALYSIS
sections.text:
A schematic of the ME device based on the piezoelectric bimorph cantilever and the tip magnet is presented in Fig. 1(a). When the ME device is placed in a non-uniform AC magnetic field generated by a typical power line, both forcemode and torque-mode excitations will be generated by the magnetic coupling of the alternating magnetic field and the magnetization of the permanent magnet. As a result, polarization is induced in the piezoelectric layer and power can be delivered to subsequent electronic devices (e.g., wireless sensors). To quantitatively analyze the cooperative interaction between magnetic force coupling and magnetic torque coupling, we use a lumped equivalent circuit model19–21 for the mass-spring-damping system and theoretically analyze the magneto-mechanical coupling, which offers an insight into the appropriate use of the compound interaction effect.

![](images/3d99e05ab2a24430af6e153bbb102153b70ad49b1eebb519f7b5fdf998e875fe.jpg)  
FIG. 1. (a) Schematic of ME energy harvester; (b) side view of experimental setup with definition of variables; (c) lumped equivalent circuit model.

The center of the power-line’s cross-section is designated as the origin of the coordinates. The $x$ -axis and the $y$ -axis are as defined in Fig. 1(b). We assume that the transverse vibration of the piezoelectric cantilever is small and that the overall mass-spring-damping system is linear. The power line is long enough to justify the assumption that the AC magnetic field distribution is consistent along the length direction of the power line. The problem can be reduced to a two-dimensional field analysis. If we consider that the permeability of the permanent magnet (e.g., a NdFeB magnet) is very close to the permeability of vacuum, it can then be assumed that the existence of the magnet in the space does little to change to the AC magnetic field distribution. As a result, the flux density in the space can be calculated using the Biot–Savart law.

$$
\mathbf { B } _ { e } = \mu \mathbf { H } _ { e } = \frac { \mu x I _ { l i n e } } { 2 \pi ( x ^ { 2 } + y ^ { 2 } ) } \mathbf { e } _ { x } - \frac { \mu y I _ { l i n e } } { 2 \pi ( x ^ { 2 } + y ^ { 2 } ) } \mathbf { e } _ { y } ,
$$

where $\mathbf { B } _ { e }$ is the flux density of the magnetic field at position $( x , y ) , I _ { l i n e }$ is the current amplitude in the power line, $\mu$ is the permeability of the NdFeB magnet, and $\mathbf { e } _ { x }$ , and $\mathbf { e } _ { y }$ are the unit vectors in the $x$ -direction and in the $y$ -direction, respectively.

The magnetic torque $\Delta \tau$ and the magnetic force vector DF that the small permanent magnet located at $( x , y )$ experiences under an external magnetic field with a flux density of $\mathbf { B } _ { e }$ are given in Ref. 22 and are expressed as

$$
\Delta \tau = | \Delta \mathbf { m } \times \mathbf { B } _ { e } | = \frac { \mu M I _ { l i n e } y \Delta x \Delta y \Delta z } { 2 \pi ( x ^ { 2 } + y ^ { 2 } ) } ,
$$

where $\Delta \mathbf { m } , M , \Delta x , \Delta y$ , and $\Delta z$ are the magnetic moment, magnetization, length, thickness, and width of the small magnet element, respectively, and

$$
\Delta \mathbf { F } = \nabla ( \Delta \mathbf { m } \cdot \mathbf { B } _ { e } ) = \frac { \partial ( \Delta \mathbf { m } \cdot \mathbf { B } _ { e } ) } { \partial x } \mathbf { e } _ { x } + \frac { \partial ( \Delta \mathbf { m } \cdot \mathbf { B } _ { e } ) } { \partial y } \mathbf { e } _ { y } .
$$

Based on the transverse vibration, the effective component of magnetic force for the excitation corresponds to the $y$ -component, $\Delta F _ { y }$ , which can be expressed as

$$
\Delta F _ { y } = \frac { \partial ( \Delta \mathbf { m } \cdot \mathbf { B } _ { e } ) } { \partial y } = \frac { \mu M I _ { l i n e } x y \Delta x \Delta y \Delta z } { \pi \left( x ^ { 2 } + y ^ { 2 } \right) ^ { 2 } } .
$$

Therefore, the magnetic torque $\tau$ and the effective force component $F _ { y }$ that are experienced by a permanent magnet centered at $( x _ { 0 } , y _ { 0 } , z _ { 0 } )$ can be calculated via the integration of Eqs. (2) and (4), which can be expressed as

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } {  { \tau = \int _ { x _ { 2 } } ^ { x _ { 1 } } \int _ { y _ { 2 } } ^ { y _ { 1 } } \int _ { z _ { 2 } } ^ { z _ { 1 } } \frac { \mu M _ { I i n e y } } { 2 \pi ( x ^ { 2 } + y ^ { 2 } ) } d x d y d z } } \\ & { } & { = \frac { \mu M M H _ { I i n e } } { 4 \pi } \bigg [ x _ { 1 } \ln \big ( x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } \big ) - x _ { 2 } \ln \big ( x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } \big ) - x _ { 1 } \ln \big ( x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \big ) } \\ & { } & { \quad + x _ { 2 } \ln \big ( x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \big ) + 2 y _ { 1 } \bigg ( \arctan \frac { x _ { 1 } } { y _ { 1 } } - \arctan \frac { x _ { 2 } } { y _ { 1 } } \bigg ) } \\ & { } & { \quad - 2 y _ { 2 } \bigg ( \arctan \frac { x _ { 1 } } { y _ { 2 } } - \arctan \frac { x _ { 2 } } { y _ { 2 } } \bigg ) \bigg ] , } \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array} { c } { { F _ { y } = \displaystyle { \int _ { x _ { 2 } } ^ { x _ { 1 } } \int _ { y _ { 2 } } ^ { y _ { 1 } } \int _ { z _ { 2 } } ^ { z _ { 1 } } \frac { \mu M I _ { l i n e } x y } { \pi \left( x ^ { 2 } + y ^ { 2 } \right) ^ { 2 } } } d x d y d z } } \\ { { = \displaystyle { \frac { \mu M w I _ { l i n e } } { 4 \pi } \mathrm { l n } \frac { \left( x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \right) \left( x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } \right) } { \left( x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } \right) \left( x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \right) } } , } } \end{array}
$$

where $x _ { 1 } = x _ { 0 } + L / 2 , x _ { 2 } = x _ { 0 } - L / 2 , y _ { 1 } = y _ { 0 } + h / 2 , y _ { 2 } = y _ { 0 }$ $- h / 2 , z _ { 1 } = z _ { 0 } + w / 2 , z _ { 2 } = z _ { 0 } - w / 2$ , and $M , L , w$ , and $h$ are the magnetization, length, width, and thickness of the permanent magnet, respectively. The variables $x _ { 0 }$ and $y _ { 0 }$ , which are the coordinates of the tip magnet center relative to the AC power line, are designated the horizontal displacement and the vertical displacement, respectively.

An approach from the literature19 of using an equivalent force that has the same effect on the cantilever deflection to replace the magnetic torque is adopted here to study the compound interaction effect. The equivalent force, $F _ { e q }$ which corresponds to the magnetic torque $\tau$ , is calculated to be $F _ { e q } = 3 \tau / 2 l _ { e f f }$ . Because the transverse vibration of the piezoelectric cantilever is small and the system is assumed to be linear, the excitations that are exerted on the piezoelectric cantilever tip can be superposed and then estimated based on the resulting effective force, $\boldsymbol { F _ { s } } = \boldsymbol { F _ { y } } + \boldsymbol { F _ { e q } }$ .

The transduction from magnetic energy to electrical energy based on the ME energy harvester can be evaluated using the lumped equivalent circuit model presented in Fig. 1(c). The converted power consumed by the load can be expressed as

$$
P _ { L } = \frac { \varphi _ { M m } ^ { 2 } \varphi _ { m e } ^ { 2 } I _ { l i n e } ^ { 2 } \left. Z _ { e } \right. ^ { 2 } } { R _ { L } \left. b + j \omega m _ { e f f } + k / j \omega + \varphi _ { m e } ^ { 2 } Z _ { e } \right. ^ { 2 } } ,
$$

where $m _ { e f f } , k$ , and $b$ are the effective mass, the spring stiffness, and the damping coefficient of the mass-spring-damping system of the cantilever beam with the tip magnet, respectively. $P _ { L }$ is the output power, $R _ { L }$ is the load resistance, and $Z _ { e }$ is the overall impedance (including the impedance of the piezoelectric cantilever and the load resistance $R _ { L } )$ , expressed as

$$
Z _ { e } = { \frac { R _ { L } ( R _ { 0 } + 1 / j \omega C _ { 0 } ) } { R _ { L } + R _ { 0 } + 1 / j \omega C _ { 0 } } } ,
$$

where $R _ { 0 }$ and $C _ { 0 }$ are the internal resistance and the capacitance of the piezoelectric cantilever, respectively. The coefficient $\varphi _ { m e }$ is the mechano-electric coupling factor, which is defined as $\varphi _ { m e } = d _ { 3 1 } ( h - h _ { p } ) / s _ { 3 3 } ^ { E }$ for the $d _ { 3 1 }$ mode and $\varphi _ { m e } = d _ { 3 3 } ( h - h _ { p } ) h _ { p } / s _ { 3 3 } ^ { E } l _ { e }$ for the $d _ { 3 3 }$ mode, where $h$ is the thickness of the piezoelectric bimorph, $h _ { p }$ is the thickness of a single piezoelectric layer, $s _ { 3 3 } ^ { E }$ is the compliance constant in the length direction, $d _ { 3 1 }$ and $d _ { 3 3 }$ are the piezoelectric constants for the $d _ { 3 1 }$ mode and the $d _ { 3 3 }$ mode, respectively, and $l _ { e }$ is the distance between adjacent interdigitated electrodes $\left( d _ { 3 3 } \right.$ mode only). By considering the nonuniform field distribution with position, the magneto-mechanical coupling factor $\varphi _ { M m }$ , which represents the mechanical excitation under the influence of a unit-strength magnetic source, is evaluated in terms of the ratio between the equivalent excitation force and the source (i.e., $I _ { l i n e } )$ of the AC magnetic field.

When the applied load is constant, the converted power given by Eq. (7) is mainly influenced by the magnetomechanical coupling factor $\varphi _ { M m }$ , and this is also the case with the ME response of the energy harvester. Therefore, the compound magnetic coupling effect can be compared with the two conventional magnetic coupling modes in terms of their corresponding magneto-mechanical coupling factors. The coefficients $\varphi _ { M m \left( \mathrm { T } \right) }$ , $\varphi _ { M m \left( \mathrm { F } \right) }$ , and $\varphi _ { M m } \left( \mathrm { F - T } \right)$ corresponding to the torque mode, the force mode, and the compound interaction mode, respectively, are presented as

$$
\varphi _ { M m ( \mathrm { T } ) } = \frac { 3 \mu M w } { 8 \pi l _ { e f f } } \mathrm { l n } \frac { \left( x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \right) \left( x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } \right) } { \left( x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } \right) \left( x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \right) } ,
$$

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \displaystyle \varphi _ { M m ( \mathrm { F } ) } = \frac { \mu M w } { 4 \pi } \biggl [ x _ { 1 } \ln \bigl ( x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } \bigr ) - x _ { 2 } \ln \bigl ( x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } \bigr ) } \\ { \displaystyle \qquad - x _ { 1 } \ln \bigl ( x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \bigr ) + x _ { 2 } \ln \bigl ( x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + y _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \bigr ) } \\ { \displaystyle \qquad + 2 y _ { 1 } \biggl ( \arctan \frac { x _ { 1 } } { y _ { 1 } } - \arctan \frac { x _ { 2 } } { y _ { 1 } } \biggr ) } \\ { \displaystyle \qquad - 2 y _ { 2 } \biggl ( \arctan \frac { x _ { 1 } } { y _ { 2 } } - \arctan \frac { x _ { 2 } } { y _ { 2 } } \biggr ) \biggr ] , } \end{array}
$$

$$
\varphi _ { M m ( \mathrm { F - T } ) } = \varphi _ { M m ( \mathrm { F } ) } + \varphi _ { M m ( \mathrm { T } ) } .
$$

Equation (11) indicates that the overall excitation is reinforced in areas where the magnetic force and the effective force of the generated torque are oriented in the same direction, and correspondingly weakened in areas where the magnetic force counteracts the torque-mode excitation. As a result, the compound interaction mode can easily outperform the conventional modes when the magnetic force and the torque cooperate. In addition, the normalized magnitude of the coupling factor $\varphi _ { M m } \mathrm { ( F - T ) }$ , which is presented in Fig. 2, shows that the compound interaction mode is heavily dependent on the positioning of the ME device. When the horizontal displacement is positive, the cooperation between the forcemode and torque-mode excitations leads to enhanced magneto-mechanical coupling, and the compound effect reaches a maximum where the horizontal displacement is $6 . 4 8 \mathrm { m m }$ . Consequently, maximized values of the ME coupling and the power conversion can be pursued in the optimal position of the compound magnetic coupling mode. When the horizontal displacement is negative, the counterproductive effect is observed, and the magneto-mechanical coupling factor is minimized with a horizontal displacement of $- 3 . 8 1 \mathrm { m m }$ , and thus the ME response and power conversion are minimized.

![](images/c08a1487f9ba282343a51ab92a6f2819292411830092090edc4ef86a679dfd80.jpg)  
FIG. 2. Normalized magnitude of theoretical magneto-mechanical coupling factor for the compound interaction mode.

sections.heading: III. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.text: Schematics of the ME device and the experimental setup used are presented in Fig. 1. A prototype ME energy harvester has been fabricated to study ME coupling and power conversion based on the proposed compound interaction mode. The energy harvester uses a typical cantilever structure. A 38 (length) $\times 1 4$ $( \mathrm { w i d t h } ) \times 1 . 1$ (thickness) $\mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ piezoelectric fiber composite bimorph composed of two 0.3- mm-thick piezoelectric fiber layers (electrically connected in parallel) and one $0 . 5 \mathrm { - m m }$ -thick stainless steel layer is used as the piezoelectric cantilever, and a 13 (length) $\times 3 0$ $\mathrm { ( w i d t h ) \times 1 0 }$ (thickness) $\mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ NdFeB N38 magnet $( 3 0 . 5 \mathrm { g } )$ is used as the permanent magnet tip mass, and is bonded at the free end of the piezoelectric cantilever. The piezofiber layer (PZT-5A) operates in the $d _ { 3 3 }$ mode with the employment of interdigitated electrodes. The piezoelectric coefficient $d _ { 3 3 }$ is $3 8 0 \ \mathrm { p C / N } ,$ , its electro-mechanical coupling factor $k _ { 3 3 }$ is 0.72, and the relative dielectric constant of the piezofiber is 1725. The energy harvester is located beneath a current-carrying power line with the permanent magnet magnetization oriented along the $y$ -axis. A DOSF-series power amplifier from Matsusada Inc. is used as the current source to provide a $1 0 \mathrm { A }$ current at $5 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , and the current magnitude is monitored using a Hall current probe. The resonance-frequency of the energy harvester has been tuned to $5 0 \mathrm { H z }$ for enhanced ME coupling and power conversion under the powerfrequency magnetic field generated by the power line. The horizontal and vertical displacements were varied with $1 \mathrm { m m }$ steps to study the position-dependent compound coupling effect.

sections.heading: IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
The ME response and the power conversion performance of the fabricated device are measured in terms of the magnetically induced electric field and the power density, and the corresponding experimental results are presented in Figs. 3 and 4, respectively. Remarkable variations in both the ME response and the power conversion can be observed in a small region. The experimentally measured ME response in Fig. 3, in particular, is similar to the theoretical magnetomechanical coupling factor in Fig. 2, which is consistent with the theoretical prediction. For certain specific vertical displacements, the peaks of the ME coefficient and the power density do not correspond with the zero horizontal displacement $( x _ { 0 } = 0 )$ ) where the magnetic torque is maximized, and the peak values are well above those that occur at $x _ { 0 } = 0$ . When the horizontal displacement is positive, the position-dependent magnetic force under the non-uniform

![](images/a26abc4c73a9979cabd0000d05a5b5a0350dfbf943d71c18267ffaf15ae05010.jpg)  
FIG. 3. Dependence of the magnetically induced electric field (MIEF) on the placement of the ME energy harvester, measured at resonance under open-circuit conditions.

AC magnetic field has a positive effect on the magnetomechanical coupling. As predicted, the pure magnetic torque mode is far from the optimal option for use in magnetoelasto-electric devices that involve magnetic coupling in non-uniform stray magnetic fields.

We use the established theoretical model to analyze the remarkable variations in ME coupling and power conversion. Because the ME coupling is dominated by the magnetomechanical coupling factor, the position required for the most efficient magnetoelectric power conversion for each coupling mode can be predicted theoretically using the derivatives of the corresponding coefficients $\varphi _ { M m }$ in Eqs. (5)–(7). Here, we set the vertical displacement $y _ { 0 }$ to be constant, and the optimal horizontal displacement that corresponds to the maximum magneto-mechanical coupling can be mathematically deduced using $\mathrm { d } \varphi _ { M m \left( \mathrm { F } \right) } = 0 , \ \mathrm { d } \varphi _ { M m \left( \mathrm { T } \right) } = 0$ and $\mathrm { d } \varphi _ { M m ( \mathrm { F - T } ) } = 0$ , respectively. The dependence of the theoretical optimal value of $x _ { 0 }$ on different $y _ { 0 }$ is shown in Fig. 5(a). The magnetic force is a result of the Zeeman energy’s position dependence on position, and thus is closely related to the flux gradient, which explains the trend of the optimal $x _ { 0 }$ to increase with increasing $y _ { 0 }$ . However, only the $y$ -component of magnetic force is effective, and as a result, the optimal value of $x _ { 0 }$ corresponding to the maximized $\varphi _ { M m \left( \mathrm { F } \right) }$ differs slightly from the value that corresponds to the maximum magnetic force. The magnetic torque, which is caused by the forced alignment of the magnetic moment of the permanent magnet with the external magnetic field, always reaches its maximum value at $x _ { 0 } = 0$ , where the magnetic moment is oriented perpendicularly to the alternating magnetic field. In addition, because the magnetic force at $x _ { 0 } = 0$ is zero, the excitation at these points is determined purely by the torque coupling mode. For the compound magnetic coupling effect, the optimal position for magneto-mechanical coupling falls in between the optimal positions for the magnetic force and the magnetic torque coupling, and lies closer to the one that has the dominant effect as the outcome of the mutual interaction. For the experimental results, the horizontal displacements $x _ { 0 }$ that correspond to the maximum power conversion agree well with the optimal positions for the theoretically derived maximum magneto-mechanical coupling factor, uMm ðF–TÞ.

![](images/208f2de05d6b98bb8c865a88954c1d98c7029b33bb0059c5cc3d1f6239960317.jpg)  
FIG. 4. Dependence of the converted power density on the placement of the ME energy harvester, measured at resonance condition in load-carrying experiment. The resistance $( 9 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ in use corresponds to the optimal load of the energy harvester.

The square of the normalized coefficients $\varphi _ { M m } \left( \mathrm { F - T } \right)$ from theory and the experimentally measured power outputs with varying horizontal displacement $x _ { 0 }$ and constant vertical displacement $( y _ { 0 } = 1 0 \mathrm { m m } )$ are presented in Fig. 5(b). It is observed that the variation trends for both the theoretically derived $\varphi _ { M m ( \mathrm { F - T } ) } ^ { 2 }$ and the experimentally measured ME device output power are consistent, which demonstrates the relationship between power conversion and the magnetomechanical coupling coefficient given in Eq. (7). The magneto-mechanical coupling is intensified because of the cooperative interaction with positive values of $x _ { 0 }$ , yielding enhanced ME power conversion. The power conversion is maximized when the horizontal displacement $x _ { 0 }$ is $6 \mathrm { m m }$ , and this value agrees well with the theoretically derived displacement of $6 . 4 8 \mathrm { m m }$ for optimal magneto-mechanical coupling. In contrast, a negative $x _ { 0 }$ leads to reduced power conversion caused by the contradiction effect, which is indicated by the small coefficient $\varphi _ { M m ( \mathrm { F - T } ) }$ . The harvested power reaches a minimum at $x _ { 0 } = - 4 \mathrm { m m }$ (which is close to the $- 3 . 8 1 \mathrm { m m }$ value for the loosest coupling obtained using the theoretical model), where the intensities of the two coupling modes are similar. Therefore, the close relationship between power conversion and the magneto-mechanical coupling is validated, and the consistency between the theoretical analysis and the experimental results verifies the rationality of the theoretical model, which can effectively predict the feature points required for the specified properties (whether enhanced or weakened).

![](images/d522419ba3a863679ec3303e601f3283bb05075cce178f242daee5134655c621.jpg)  
FIG. 5. (a) Optimal placements from theory with regard to different magnetic coupling modes and experimentally measured positions for maximized power conversion; (b) dependence of theoretically derived magnetomechanical coupling factor and experimentally measured power output on the horizontal displacement $x _ { 0 }$ for the constant vertical displacement $( y _ { 0 } = 1 0 \mathrm { m m } )$ ).

The theoretical model also provides an effective way to account for the dramatically enhanced ME transduction. For ease of comparison, we introduce the normalized power output in the form $\bar { P } _ { L } = P _ { L } / P _ { L 0 }$ , where $P _ { L 0 }$ is the maximum output power based on optimal cooperative magnetic coupling at $y _ { 0 } = 8 \mathrm { m m }$ . With the variation in the vertical displacement $y _ { 0 }$ , the normalized maximum output power from theory with respect to the different modes is presented in Fig. 6(a).

Because the magnetic force is heavily dependent on the gradient of the flux density, the power conversion based on the force mode decays dramatically with increasing $y _ { 0 }$ . The magnetic torque is proportional to the flux density, which has a rate of change depending on the displacement variation much smaller than that of the flux gradient. Therefore, the magnetic torque mode performs more efficiently than the force mode at a moderate distance from the magnetic field source, which is consistent with the conclusion given in Ref. 19. In comparison, efficient power conversion can be guaranteed over the entire displacement range when based on the compound magnetic coupling effect. Additionally, the optimal locations and the maximum magneto-mechanical coupling factors of the different modes with respect to a certain vertical displacement are usually determined, which can be analyzed based on Eqs. (9)–(11). As a result, the ratio between the maximum power outputs for any two coupling modes can also be determined and is mainly dependent on the size of the harvester. Fig. 6(b) presents the experimental results for the harvested power with respect to various vertical displacements based on the torque mode and the discovered coupling mode. When the ME energy harvester is placed $1 0 \mathrm { m m }$ beneath a 10 Arms power line, the maximum harvested power based on purely magnetic torque coupling is $2 7 3 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W }$ . At the optimal position $( x _ { 0 } = 6 \mathrm { m m }$ $y _ { 0 } = 1 0 \mathrm { m m } )$ for the compound magnetic coupling effect, the power output of the energy harvester is dramatically enhanced to $2 . 1 3 6 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ , which is 7.8 times the value based on the torque mode alone. Despite being at a greater distance from the power line, the ME energy harvester based on the compound magnetic coupling mode has proved to be capable of harvesting much higher power than existing energy harvesters based on magnetic force coupling under the same conducting current conditions.17,18 The improved power conversion offered by the cooperative effect enhances the possibility of the ME energy harvester being used as a noninvasive and reliable power supply for ubiquitous wireless sensor nodes in both residential and industrial applications. From a more general perspective, the compound magnetic coupling effect represents an effective way to reinforce magneto-mechanical coupling when pursuing enhanced ME devices properties (e.g., increased sensitivity and power density) under non-uniform stray magnetic fields.

![](images/845669990e6f0acbe2e3bbd0c9f51d26486c2c6ee5c4e13e4f84421a01908539.jpg)  
FIG. 6. (a) Normalized harvested power based on different magnetic coupling modes from theory; (b) experimental results for the harvested power based on the magnetic torque coupling mode and the compound magnetic coupling mode.

sections.heading: V. CONCLUSION
sections.text: In summary, we have theoretically predicted and experimentally demonstrated the compound magnetic coupling effect, which is rooted in the subtle interplay between an alternating magnetic field and the tip permanent magnet of a cantilever-structured ME device. The cooperative interaction between the magnetic torque coupling and the magnetic force coupling reinforces the overall excitation, thus enhancing the ME response and greatly boosting the power conversion of ME devices. Our established theoretical model has proved to be effective for quantitative interpretation of the interaction principle and predicting the optimal arrangement required for maximized ME devices performance. The superiority of the proposed compound magnetic coupling mode over the conventional individual modes is demonstrated by a great improvement in the output power of the piezoelectric/magnet energy harvester. This enhanced power conversion means that the ME energy harvester is more likely to be able to scavenge energy from low-frequency magnetic fields to realize selfpowered, maintenance-free wireless sensor networks.
